evidence: Cic. Fam. 7.32.1: quōcum mihi est magnus ūsus
Cic. Rosc. Am. 15: domesticus ūsus et cōnsuētūdō (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Its first sense is use or practice; of people, the intercourse and familiarity of those who deal with each other often (Lewis & Short): mihi cum eō magnus ūsus est, “I have a lot to do with him”. Often paired with cōnsuētūdō, being much together (see company).

evidence: Plaut. Aul. 4.4.4: quid tibi mēcum est commercī, senex? (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Tusc. 5.66: commercium habēre cum Mūsīs (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: First trade, commerce; then any dealings or communication: mihi cum vostrīs lēgibus nihil est commercī, “I have nothing to do with your laws” (Plaut. Rud. 3.4.20, Lewis & Short).
A friendly meeting or conversation, in the plural social contact; also a hostile encounter, a clash (Lewis & Short). See meeting.

terms.grammar: phrase, with a verb: inter sē colloquī, inter sē dīligere
terms.comment: Latin says “interact” with a verb of what is done and inter sē, “with one another” (see each other).

phrases.english: with whom I have a great deal to do
